title: The opening stanza and its revisions
short: FitzGerald's sequence opens with a dawn summons; this is the fifth-edition (1889) text, very different from the first edition's 'Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night'.
body: Edward FitzGerald (1809-83) published his free English version of quatrains attributed to the Persian mathematician-poet Omar Khayyam (1048-1131) anonymously in 1859, and revised it for editions in 1868, 1872 and 1879; the fifth edition (1889) appeared after his death. The 1859 stanza read: 'Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night / Has flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight: / And Lo! the Hunter of the East has caught / The Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light.' The second edition began 'Wake! For the Sun behind yon Eastern height'; the form printed here was reached in 1872 and kept thereafter. FitzGerald called it 'the infernal Stanza I' and in 1872 asked his teacher E. B. Cowell for help with it.

title: The ruba'i stanza
short: Each stanza imitates the Persian ruba'i: four lines rhyming AABA, here in iambic pentameter, with the unrhymed third line building towards the last.
body: The Persian ruba'i is a quatrain in a special family of metres, rhyming aaba (sometimes aaaa), and is complete in itself; collections are arranged alphabetically by rhyme, not as a narrative. FitzGerald kept the rhyme scheme (flight / Night / Light, with 'strikes' unrhymed) in English iambic pentameter, and the third line's suspension gives each stanza a turn before the clinching fourth, a structure later poets imitated. He also arranged his quatrains into a loose day-long sequence from dawn to moonrise, which has no basis in the Persian collections.

title: The Sun and its Persian source
greek: Persian Kai-Khusraw-i ruz ('the Kai Khusraw of day'), garbled in the Calcutta copy as ganjar-i ruz
short: Arberry traces the stanza to Calcutta quatrain 137; FitzGerald worked from a garbled copy of its royal sun and used only the first half.
body: FitzGerald worked from two manuscripts sent by Cowell: the Ouseley manuscript in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (copied 1460), and a later manuscript belonging to the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, now lost. According to Arberry, the source of stanza I is Calcutta quatrain 137, which pictures dawn as the sun casting a stone into the cup and a herald (munadi) crying to the drinkers to fill their cups. In the Calcutta copy the phrase for the sun, 'the Kai Khusraw of day' (Kai-Khusraw-i ruz), was garbled so that it seems to read ganjar-i ruz; FitzGerald looked up ganjar ('rouge') and conjectured a 'rouged' day, which fed the first edition's wording, and he dropped the second half of the quatrain. The conquering Sun of the final text, scattering the stars and driving Night before it, keeps the Persian royal-military picture.

title: The Field of Night
short: Night is a battlefield ('field' in the military sense), from which the Sun routs the Stars like a defeated army.
body: 'Field' here is the field of battle (OED, field n. sense 'the ground on which a battle is fought'), and 'scatter'd into flight' is the language of rout. The conceit is of a royal conqueror at dawn who first puts the Stars to flight and then 'Drives Night along with them'. FitzGerald's revisions made the image steadily more martial and more unified: the 1859 version mixed a drinking-bowl, a thrown stone and a hunter's noose, while the final text holds to one metaphor of a king in battle. Readers have debated whether the gain in coherence lost the original's oriental strangeness.

title: 'strikes': the stone in the cup
short: The first edition's 'flung the Stone' recalled a custom FitzGerald explained in a note: a stone thrown into a cup was the desert signal 'To Horse!'
body: FitzGerald's note to stanza I, kept in later editions, explains: 'Flinging a Stone into the Cup was the signal for To Horse! in the Desert.' The 1859 Morning had 'flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight'; in the final version the striking passes to the Sun's 'Shaft of Light'. The custom has been traced to Persian dictionaries, and possibly to the Shahnama's striking of a ball or stone on a bell-like vessel carried by an elephant, but the evidence is unclear. In Baqi's elegy for Suleyman, also in this archive, a stone thrown into the beaker is likewise the signal that the party is over.

title: The Sultan's Turret
short: The first rays touch the highest point of the palace: dawn reaches the king's tower before the town below.
body: The image is visual, the sun's first light catching the top of a palace tower, but it also sets the Sun above earthly kings: even the Sultan's turret is struck by a greater monarch. This line survives unchanged from 1859 ('The Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light'), and FitzGerald capitalises the nouns throughout, a habit that gives the poem its slightly archaic, emblematic look. The sultan, palace and turret belong to the Victorian Orient as much as to Seljuk Nishapur; Omar lived under Seljuk sultans, one of whom, Malik-Shah, employed him on calendar reform.

title: 'Shaft of Light' and the 'Noose of Light'
short: The ray is an arrow; in 1859 it was a hunter's 'Noose of Light', the lasso (kamand) of Persian heroic and lyric poetry.
body: 'Shaft' means both an arrow and a beam of light (OED, shaft n.1), so the word completes the military image of the Sun as an archer. The first edition's 'Hunter of the East' who 'caught / The Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light' drew on a more distinctively Persian image, the lasso (kamand) with which heroes in the Shahnama capture enemies and with which, in lyric, the beloved's curls catch lovers. Decker's edition shows that the revision to 'Shaft of Light' came with the second edition (1868).

title: The dawn summons
short: The stanza sets the poem's day in motion: a call to wake and seize the day, which the next stanzas turn into a call to drink.
body: FitzGerald built his sequence on the shape of one day, from this dawn to the rising moon of the last stanzas, so the summons to 'WAKE!' is both literal and thematic: life is brief and the morning must be used. The Persian source quatrain, as Arberry describes it, paired dawn with a herald calling the drinkers to the tavern; FitzGerald's next stanza (II) supplies a voice from the tavern asking why the 'drowsy Worshiper' nods outside the prepared Temple (the 1859 version had the voice cry 'Awake, my Little ones, and fill the Cup'). Victorian readers heard in this a hedonist, sceptical gospel, carpe diem rather than the call to prayer that dawn means in a Muslim city.
